rows.explanation: Change B adds a 60s in-memory cache for GET /api/tags and invalidates it only when articles are created with tags. Change A makes article deletion remove orphaned tags from the database but does not invalidate the cache. After merge, deleting an article whose tags become orphaned deletes the tags in the DB, yet GET /api/tags continues to serve the stale cached list (including removed tags) for up to 60 seconds. The cache invariant assumed by B (tag set only changes on article creation) is broken by A's new tag deletion path.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes userUpdatePrisma hash any password passed to it. Change B's new userChangePassword controller already hashes the new password with hashPassword before calling userUpdatePrisma. After merging, the change-password endpoint hashes twice: userUpdatePrisma hashes the already-hashed value. The stored password is hash(hash(newPassword)), so the user can no longer log in with their new password, because login compares the plain password against the double hash. B's tests still pass, since they only check that the stored value differs from the plain text and from the previous hash, which a double hash satisfies. A's tests only exercise PUT /api/user, which doesn't hit the double hashing. The two changes also both fix plain-text password storage, in different layers.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds Prisma's @updatedAt to Article.updatedAt and removes the manual updatedAt set in articleUpdatePrisma. Change B adds a views counter that is incremented via prisma.article.update on every article GET. With @updatedAt, any prisma.article.update call (including B's views increment) automatically bumps updatedAt, so merely reading an article now changes its updatedAt timestamp, making it appear modified. Neither change alone has this effect: before A, B's increment would not touch updatedAt; before B, A's @updatedAt only fired on real edits. The merged behavior is wrong in a concrete way, since updatedAt no longer reflects content edits.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem: after an article is deleted, tags no longer used by any article should not appear in GET /api/tags. Change A does it by deleting orphaned tags from the database at article-delete time; Change B does it by filtering unused tags out at read time in getTags. Each alone satisfies the identical scenario (even the two added tests are nearly identical). Merged, the work is duplicated: the read-time filter becomes redundant (or the cleanup becomes unnecessary), so one of the two should be removed. There are also semantic differences (A permanently deletes orphan tags, including ones that never had articles; B only hides them), making the merged behavior contradictory in design.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes fix the same bug: the article feed returning articles from all authors instead of only followed ones. Change A filters in the Prisma query (where author.followedBy some username), while Change B filters in the controller after the query using currentUser.follows. Merged, the feed is filtered twice, which is redundant but correct, and each change also adds its own duplicate test for the same behavior. Since both solve the same problem in different ways, one filter (and one test) should be removed. Change B's post-query filter is also the buggier approach, because applying it after limit/offset pagination can return short pages, which Change A's query-level filter already avoids.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes fix the same bug (missing ownership check on article deletion) in two different ways: Change A adds an inline author check inside the articlesDelete controller, while Change B adds a requireArticleAuthor middleware on the DELETE route that performs the identical lookup and 403 response. Merged, every delete request runs the check twice (two extra DB lookups of user and article), and the ownership logic lives in two places that can drift apart. One of the two implementations should be removed. Both also delete the same known-bug test and add near-duplicate new tests.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A truncates generated slugs to 100 characters inside slugfy. Change B caps the title length at 150 in the create validator. Both address overly long titles/slugs, but at different layers and for different purposes. A bounds the derived slug, while B rejects overly long inputs. They do not contradict: titles up to 150 characters are accepted, and their slugs are truncated to 100. B's test uses 'x'.repeat(150), and the slug would just be truncated, so the 201 still holds. There is a slight collision risk if two long titles share the first 100 characters, but that is a pre-existing concern of A alone and not caused by B. No concrete failure or duplicated work arises from the combination.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds database indexes on Article.authorUsername and Article.updatedAt in the Prisma schema. Change B adds a sort query parameter (created/updated) to the article list endpoint, ordering by createdAt or updatedAt. They touch different layers and do not interfere. The updatedAt index even supports the default sort in B. Sorting by createdAt has no index, which is only a performance matter and not a correctness issue. Neither change solves the same problem as the other, and no runtime assumption is broken.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A caches the tag list and invalidates it via a prisma.$use middleware on writes to Tag or Article (including deleteMany on Tag). Change B adds a prisma.tag.deleteMany after article deletion. That deleteMany on model Tag triggers A's middleware (action deleteMany, model Tag), so the cache is cleared, and the article delete itself invalidates too. The two work correctly together: deleting an article removes orphan tags and the cache is dropped, so GET /api/tags will not show stale deleted tags. The only gap is raw queries, which A deliberately treats as non-writes, and B does not use them. No concrete failure scenario arises, and the changes address different problems (caching vs orphan cleanup).

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes address password handling after a password update, but via different paths. Change A fixes the plain-text password bug in the existing PUT /api/user flow by hashing in userUpdatePrisma. Change B adds a new POST /api/user/password endpoint that hashes through its own userSetPasswordPrisma and does not touch userUpdatePrisma. B's endpoint hashes at the controller level and does not call userUpdatePrisma, so no double hashing occurs, and A's hashing only applies to the update path. At runtime they coexist correctly. On intent, though, B's endpoint does not claim to fix the bug in PUT /api/user; it is a new feature (with current password verification), and the PUT path remains separate, so they don't duplicate the same fix. Both now offer ways to change a password, but that is a design overlap rather than duplicated or contradictory logic.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A renames JWT_SECRET to AUTH_JWT_SECRET across the code and in .env.test. Change B adds password reset tokens that use only RESET_TOKEN_SECRET and never reference JWT_SECRET, plus one new line in .env.test. The two .env.test edits touch different lines, so they merge cleanly. Combined, .env.test has AUTH_JWT_SECRET and RESET_TOKEN_SECRET, and every reference to JWT_SECRET has been renamed. B's code and tests depend only on RESET_TOKEN_SECRET, which remains present, so nothing breaks. The two changes solve different problems and neither relies on an assumption the other breaks.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A lowers the default page size in articlesListPrisma from 20 to 10 so that plain GET /api/articles returns at most 10 articles. Change B adds ?page=N to the controller and hardcodes PAGE_SIZE = 20, always passing limit=20 and offset=(page-1)*20 to the DB function. A's default is only hit when limit is undefined (no page, no limit), so B's page requests are unaffected at the DB layer, and B's tests (page=1 gives 20 articles, page=2 gives 5) still pass. A's test hits the default path and gets 10. However, the merged API now has two inconsistent notions of page size: the default unpaginated list returns 10 articles, while ?page=1 returns 20. A client migrating from the default list to ?page=1 sees the page size change, and ?page=2 would skip items 11-20 relative to a default-limit view. The two changes also disagree on the intended page size (10 vs 20). This is a contradiction in intent about the page size, though each behaves correctly in isolation and no concrete crash occurs.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds a log line after successful article creation; Change B adds a tag-count validation that returns early with 422 before any creation happens. Both edit the same function but in separate regions, and they compose cleanly: rejected requests are never logged (correct, since no article was created), and accepted requests are logged as before. The tests are independent: A's test creates an article with no tags, and B's tests don't check logging. There is no shared assumption broken and no duplicated purpose.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A refactors the where clause construction in articlesListPrisma into a conditionally-built object; the behavior is equivalent (undefined filters are omitted either way) and the function signature is unchanged. Change B adds a new controller that calls articlesListPrisma(undefined, username, undefined, limit, offset), relying only on the signature and the authorUsername filter, which A preserves. No assumption is broken and the two changes do not solve the same problem.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds a comment-count endpoint for articles (/api/articles/:slug/comments/count) and Change B adds an article-count endpoint for tags (/api/tags/:tag/count). They touch different controllers, routers, and test files, and the routes are on distinct paths with no shadowing. Neither changes behavior the other relies on, and they solve different problems, so there is no runtime or intent conflict.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A only adds JSDoc comments to userUpdatePrisma and the UpdateFields interface; Change B adds trimming of bio and image inside the function body plus an integration test. The two edit different regions of the same file and merge cleanly. The doc comment ('fields left out are kept') remains accurate: B's spread sets bio/image to undefined when absent, and Prisma treats undefined as no change. The JSDoc doesn't mention trimming, but that is a minor documentation omission, not a behavioral conflict or duplicated solution.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A converts article deletion to a soft delete (sets deletedAt) and adds `deletedAt: null` filters to the article get, list and feed queries. Change B adds a new /api/tags/counts endpoint that counts articles per tag using `_count: { select: { article: true } }` on the Tag model, with no deletedAt filter. After merging, soft-deleted articles remain in the database and stay linked to their tags, so the count includes them. Scenario: Alice creates an article tagged 'x', deletes it (soft delete, row kept), and /api/tags/counts still reports x with count 1, even though no visible article uses that tag. Because B's `count > 0` filter hides tags with zero articles, a tag used only by deleted articles would wrongly still appear. Neither change is wrong alone: before A, deletes were hard and the counts were correct. This is a runtime conflict caused by A breaking the assumption B relies on, that every existing article row is a live article.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem: making email handling case- and whitespace-insensitive for register and login. Change A normalizes in the controllers via a new normalizeEmail util. Change B normalizes inside the DB helpers (userCreatePrisma and userGetEmailPrisma) with inline trim().toLowerCase(). Merged, every email is normalized twice, which is harmless at runtime (idempotent), but there are now two competing normalization mechanisms and a redundant util plus duplicate tests. One of the two approaches should be removed.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes article updates derive a new slug from the title, so slugs can now change on rename. Change B introduces a RecentView table keyed by (username, slug) with no foreign key to Article. When an article is renamed under A's behavior, the old slug rows in RecentView remain orphaned and are never updated to the new slug. Concrete scenario: bob views 'old-title' (recorded in RecentView), alice renames the article to 'New Title', and bob's /api/user/recent no longer shows that article, since recentArticlesPrisma looks up articles by the stale slug and silently drops missing ones. Also, the stale entries still occupy one of the KEEP=10 slots, crowding out valid entries. Before A, slugs were effectively immutable, so B's slug-as-stable-identifier assumption held; A breaks it.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A switches the list ordering from updatedAt to createdAt. Change B adds an ?after=<slug> cursor that filters on updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt while relying on the list being ordered by updatedAt desc (and it still orders by updatedAt in its version). Merged, the list is ordered by createdAt desc but the cursor filters by updatedAt. Concrete scenario: article X is created first but edited recently (updatedAt newest); list shows [newer(created later), X]. Requesting ?after=X gives updatedAt < X.updatedAt, which returns all other articles including 'newer' that was already shown before X, so pagination duplicates/skips items. Conversely, after=newer would exclude X (X.updatedAt > newer.updatedAt) even though X comes after newer in the list. B's own test passes only because createdAt and updatedAt orderings coincide there. This is a runtime conflict arising from the broken ordering assumption.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds an https-only rule for the image field to the PUT /api/user validator (userUpdateValidator). Change B adds a new PUT /api/user/image endpoint that sets the same image field but bypasses that validator (only authenticate + a string type check). Merged, a client can set an image like "http://..." or "javascript:..." via /api/user/image, which A's rule would reject on /api/user. The https invariant A introduces is not enforced on B's new write path. B's test uses an https URL so it passes, but the rule is inconsistent between the two paths.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes add a way to list the current user's favorited articles. Change A adds a dedicated GET /api/user/favorites endpoint, while Change B adds ?favorited=me to GET /api/articles. They solve the same problem two different ways, with near-identical tests and the same 401 behavior for unauthenticated requests, so the merged API duplicates the feature and one of the two should be removed.
